topic.ru: Три текста: почему горы перестают расти, как устроены высокоскоростные железные дороги, и спор о чтении генома у каждого новорождённого.

textTitles: Rails at three hundred kilometres an hour
Should every newborn have their genome read?

paragraphs.text: Mountains appear to be among the most permanent features of the landscape, but they are in constant motion. Most of the great ranges of the world were raised by the collision of the enormous plates that make up the outer shell of the Earth, and many are still rising today, some by several millimetres a year. At the same time they are being worn away by rain, ice, rivers and landslides. The height of a mountain range at any moment reflects the balance between these two processes, and understanding that balance has become one of the most active areas of geology. The contest between them has been going on for as long as the Earth has had continents.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The forces that push mountains up are now well understood in outline. Where two continental plates collide, neither can sink easily into the dense rock below, so the crust between them crumples and thickens, much as a rug wrinkles when it is pushed against a wall. The highest mountains on Earth were formed in this way, where one continent has been driving into another for around fifty million years, and precise satellite measurements show that parts of the range are still being pushed upwards. Earthquakes along the edges of the range are a sign that the collision is continuing.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Thickened crust behaves in a way that is less intuitive. Because the rock of the crust is lighter than the rock beneath it, a mountain range floats on the denser layer below, rather as an iceberg floats in water, with a deep root extending far beneath the visible peaks. When material is removed from the top by erosion, the whole range rises slightly in response, just as an iceberg rises when its top melts. This means that erosion does not simply lower mountains; it also helps to lift the rock beneath them towards the surface. The idea was proposed in the nineteenth century after surveyors found that mountains pulled plumb lines less than their visible size predicted.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Erosion is not uniform, and its intensity depends heavily on climate. In mountains with heavy rainfall, rivers cut deep valleys rapidly and trigger frequent landslides, while glaciers in colder ranges grind their beds and carry away enormous quantities of rock. Some geologists have argued that glaciers act as a kind of limit on mountain height: above the level at which ice forms and flows, erosion becomes so rapid that peaks can rise little further, an idea sometimes described as a glacial buzzsaw. Other researchers doubt that the limit is as strict as the name suggests, since some glaciated peaks continue to rise.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The strength of rock sets another limit. Rock at the base of a very high mountain is under enormous pressure, and it becomes weaker as temperatures rise deep within the thickened crust. Beyond a certain height, the crust can no longer support additional weight and begins to spread sideways under its own load. Calculations suggest that on Earth this limit lies not far above the height of the tallest existing peaks, which may explain why no mountain is much higher, although the lower gravity of other planets allows far taller mountains there. The largest volcano known in the solar system is several times the height of the highest peak on Earth.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: One of the most surprising discoveries of recent decades is that erosion and climate can influence the movement of rock deep underground. Where heavy rainfall rapidly removes material from one side of a range, rock from depth moves upwards to replace it, and some studies suggest that this flow can concentrate uplift in particular places. The idea that the weather may help to shape the pattern of deformation within a mountain range remains debated, but it has changed the way many geologists think about the relationship between the surface and the deep Earth. Testing it is difficult, because the processes involved take place over millions of years and deep beneath the surface.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Mountains eventually stop growing when the forces that built them fade. Once the collision of plates slows or stops, erosion gradually wins, and over tens of millions of years even the highest ranges are worn down. Some ancient mountains that were once as high as any on Earth today are now low hills, and their former height can be estimated only from the types of rock exposed at the surface, which were formed at great depth and have been brought up as the material above them was stripped away. Geologists sometimes describe such landscapes as the roots of mountains.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The study of how mountains rise and fall has practical consequences. Rapidly rising and eroding ranges are prone to earthquakes and landslides, and understanding where rock is moving fastest helps to assess these hazards. Mountains also influence climate by blocking winds and forcing air upwards, where it cools and releases rain, and the erosion of mountain rock removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere through chemical reactions. On the longest timescales, the rise and decay of mountain ranges may have played a part in the great changes of climate that the Earth has experienced. Such links remain difficult to prove, but they make mountains central to the history of the planet.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: Rails at three hundred kilometres an hour

paragraphs.text: When the first dedicated high-speed railway opened in Japan in 1964, its trains ran at 210 kilometres an hour, a speed that seemed extraordinary at a time when most passenger trains elsewhere rarely exceeded 120. Today trains in several countries run routinely at 300 kilometres an hour or more, and high-speed networks connect many of the major cities of Europe and East Asia. Achieving these speeds required rethinking almost every element of the railway, from the track to the shape of the train itself. Speed alone, however, was never the only aim; reliability and safety mattered just as much. The opening line was built in time for a major international sporting event held in the capital that year.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The most fundamental change was to the line. Conventional railways followed routes laid out in the nineteenth century, with curves and gradients suited to slow steam trains. At high speed, a curve must be very gentle, or passengers are pushed sideways and the forces on the track become excessive; high-speed lines therefore have curves with radii of several kilometres and are built as far as possible in straight lines, using tunnels and viaducts to cross difficult terrain. Tracks are often laid on concrete slabs rather than the traditional bed of stones, which reduces maintenance and keeps the rails precisely aligned. Building such lines through existing towns and farmland often involves lengthy disputes over the route.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Power and signalling had to change as well. High-speed trains draw electricity from overhead wires, and at 300 kilometres an hour the contact between the wire and the collector on the roof must be maintained without interruption, which requires the wire to be kept under high tension. Drivers cannot read trackside signals reliably at such speeds, so information about the line ahead is transmitted directly to a display in the cab, and the train will brake automatically if the driver fails to respond. Many high-speed lines are also fenced along their whole length, since there are no level crossings with roads.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The train itself is designed to minimise air resistance, which rises steeply with speed and accounts for most of the energy used at high velocity. Noses are long and smoothly curved, the gaps between carriages are covered, and equipment is placed beneath the floor or in enclosed spaces rather than on the roof. The long nose also solves a problem specific to tunnels: a blunt train entering a tunnel at high speed pushes a pressure wave ahead of it that emerges from the far end with a loud bang, disturbing people living nearby. Engineers test new designs in wind tunnels and increasingly with computer simulations before any full-size train is built.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Many high-speed trains spread their motors along the length of the train rather than concentrating them in locomotives at each end. This arrangement improves acceleration and braking, because more wheels are driven, and it frees space for passengers. It also spreads the weight of the train more evenly, which reduces wear on the track. Braking itself relies heavily on the motors, which act as generators when the train slows down, returning electricity to the overhead wires for use by other trains. Mechanical brakes are used mainly at low speeds and in emergencies.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: High-speed rail competes most successfully with air travel on journeys of between about two and four hours by train. On such routes, the time saved by avoiding airport security and travel to airports outside cities can outweigh the slower journey itself. Where a fast rail link has opened between two cities previously served by frequent flights, air traffic on the route has in several cases fallen sharply, and some airlines have withdrawn their services altogether. On longer routes, flying generally remains quicker. Rail operators often emphasise that passengers can work throughout the journey, something that is harder to do on a short flight.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The costs are high. Building a new line often costs tens of millions of euros per kilometre, and much more where extensive tunnelling is required, and several projects have run far over budget. Critics argue that the same money could produce greater benefits if spent on improving local and regional services, which carry far more passengers. Supporters reply that high-speed lines free capacity on existing railways for freight and local trains and bring economic benefits to the cities they connect, although the evidence on the second point is mixed. Some countries have also found that trains running on new lines attract passengers who previously did not travel at all, rather than only those who would otherwise have flown or driven.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Engineers continue to push for higher speeds. Experimental trains have exceeded 570 kilometres an hour on conventional rails, and magnetic levitation trains, which float above a guideway without touching it, have gone faster still. In everyday service, however, speeds have largely levelled off at around 300 to 350 kilometres an hour, because above that level energy use, noise and wear increase sharply. For most operators, the priority is now reliability and frequency rather than further increases in top speed. Maintaining track and trains to the standards required at high speed also costs considerably more than on conventional railways.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: Should every newborn have their genome read?

paragraphs.text: For more than half a century, many countries have tested newborn babies for a small number of serious conditions using a few drops of blood taken from the heel. The test looks for disorders that are rare but treatable, where early diagnosis can prevent severe illness or disability. Now that the cost of reading an entire human genome has fallen dramatically, some researchers have proposed going much further: sequencing the genome of every newborn and screening it for hundreds of conditions at once. Pilot programmes in several countries are testing the idea, and the debate about whether it should become routine is intensifying. The proposal has attracted both enthusiasm and concern from doctors, scientists and parents.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Supporters point to conditions that current screening misses. Hannah Lee, a geneticist involved in one pilot, notes that there are several hundred genetic disorders for which an effective treatment exists and for which early diagnosis makes a real difference, but only a few dozen are included in standard programmes. Families of children with such conditions often spend years seeking a diagnosis, during which damage that could have been prevented occurs. Sequencing at birth, she argues, could end many of these searches before they begin. Some of these disorders affect the ability to process particular nutrients and can be managed simply by changing the diet from birth.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The difficulty lies in interpreting what is found. A genome contains millions of variations, and for many of them the consequences are uncertain. A variant associated with a disease in one family may cause no symptoms in another, and some conditions that appear in the genetic results may never develop at all. Marco Bellini, a paediatrician, warns that reporting uncertain findings can turn healthy children into patients-in-waiting, subjecting families to anxiety and repeated medical checks for problems that may never appear. The problem is greater for families whose ancestors come from populations that have been less well studied, since fewer variants in those groups have been interpreted.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Most pilot programmes have responded by limiting what they report. Rather than returning everything, they search only for variants in a defined list of genes linked to conditions that begin in childhood and can be treated or managed. Aisha Rahman, who studies the ethics of genetic testing, supports this approach but notes that the list is a matter of judgement rather than science and is likely to expand over time. She argues that parents should be told clearly what is and is not being examined, since many assume that a normal result means their child is free of all genetic risk. Several programmes review their lists every year in the light of new evidence.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Consent and the future use of the data raise further questions. A genome sequenced at birth could in principle be reanalysed throughout life as knowledge improves, and it contains information about the relatives of the child as well as the child. Rahman points out that the child has no say in the decision and may later prefer not to know about risks of conditions that begin in adulthood. She believes that information about such conditions should be withheld until the child is old enough to decide for themselves. Storing the data securely for decades is itself a significant technical and legal challenge.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The costs extend well beyond the sequencing itself. Peter Voss, a health economist, observes that the price of reading a genome is now only a small part of the total, which also includes analysing results, confirming findings with further tests, genetic counselling for families and follow-up care. He estimates that the health system would need many more specialists in genetics than it currently has, and he argues that the money might produce greater benefits if spent on expanding conventional screening, whose value is already established. Training enough specialists would take many years, even if funding were available immediately.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Early results from pilot programmes offer some reassurance and some caution. In several studies, a small percentage of apparently healthy babies were found to have a condition that had not been suspected and that could be treated, a rate higher than conventional screening alone would have produced. Most parents who took part said they did not regret doing so. At the same time, uptake has been lower than researchers expected, and families from some communities have been much less likely to agree, which raises the risk that any benefits would be unequally shared. Researchers are now studying how to explain the programmes more effectively to families who are hesitant.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The question is therefore less whether genome sequencing can help newborns, which the evidence suggests it sometimes can, than whether it can be introduced in a way that is accurate, fair and affordable. Programmes that begin with a narrow list of treatable conditions, explain clearly what they do and do not examine, and invest in the specialists needed to interpret results appear to offer the most defensible path. Extending screening to every baby before those conditions are in place would risk creating more uncertainty than it resolves. The same caution has shaped the introduction of earlier forms of screening, which also expanded gradually.
paragraphs.label: H
